title: Grouping Rules and Reading a Product Term Off a Group
quickIdea: A group must be a rectangle of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells; keep the variables that are constant across it, drop the ones that change, and prefer the largest groups and the fewest of them.
remember: Group size must be a power of two - 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 - and the shape must be a rectangle or square, including the wrap-around rectangles.
Read the term by inspection: a variable that is 0 in every cell of the group appears complemented, a variable that is 1 in every cell appears plain, and a variable that takes both values is dropped.
A group of 2^k cells drops exactly k variables, so the term has n - k literals. A group of 4 in a four-variable map is a 2-literal term.
Groups may overlap, and overlapping is often required: a cell may belong to several groups, and it must belong to at least one.
Cover every 1 at least once, with the fewest groups and each as large as possible; a 1 that cannot combine is a legal group of one cell, a full minterm.
Start with the loneliest 1 - the cell with the fewest 1-neighbours - because its group is forced, and that group often determines the rest.

example.prompt: Minimise F(A,B,C,D) = Sigma m(0, 1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 12, 13) on the map.
example.work: These eight cells are 0000, 0001, 0100, 0101, 1000, 1001, 1100 and 1101: every combination of A, B and D with C = 0. They form two quads (rows AB = 00 and 01, and rows AB = 11 and 10, both in columns CD = 00 and 01), and the two quads merge into one group of eight across the A boundary. C is 0 in all eight cells; A, B and D each take both values.
example.answer: F = C', one term of one literal from eight minterms.

gateAngle: This is the mechanical core of every map question: GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q.30 is an octet that collapses to B', and GATE CSE 2012 Q.30 asks which two quads a four-1 map with don't cares admits. Both are decided by group size and by reading the constant variables.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A group of four cells in a five-variable map: how many literals has its term, and which cells could it be?
variations.answer: Three literals (5 - 2), and it could be any rectangle of four cells - for example cells 0, 1, 8 and 9, which is B'C'D'.
variations.why: The rule n - k literals holds in every map size; what changes with the size is the shape of the rectangles and whether a group can cross the reflection axis.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: In a four-variable map the cells m2, m3, m10 and m11 are 1. What is the minimal SOP?
variations.why: m2 = 0010, m3 = 0011, m10 = 1010, m11 = 1011: B = 0 and C = 1 in all four, A and D vary, so the quad is B'C - two literals from four minterms.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A function has 1s at m0, m1 and m8 only. What is its minimal SOP, and why is the answer not a group of four?
variations.answer: F = A'B'C' + B'C'D', that is the pair {m0, m1} and the pair {m0, m8}.
variations.why: m0, m1, m8 and m9 would be a quad, but m9 is 0, so the quad is illegal; the largest legal groups are the two pairs, each of three literals, and m0 is shared between them. This is the standard example of overlapping groups being necessary.

trap.what: Drawing a group of three, of six, or an L-shape, or reading the term from the map position instead of the labels.
trap.why: Only power-of-two rectangles correspond to a single product term: combining three cells would need two terms, not one. And a group's term is fixed by the variable values in its cells, not by where it sits on the page.
trap.counterexample: Cells 0, 1 and 3 are three cells and do not form one term; the minimal cover is (0,1) plus (1,3), giving A'B' + A'C - two terms, which is why the count of groups, not the count of cells, is the cost.

check.question: Read the term for the group {m0, m4, m12, m8} in a four-variable map.
check.explanation: The four cells are 0000, 0100, 1100, 1000: C = 0 and D = 0 in all four while A and B vary, so the term keeps C' and D' only. This group is the whole left-hand column pair of the map, which is why the wrap-around matters.

sources.title: Lecture 10 - Karnaugh Map and Digital Circuit Realization
sources.channel: NPTEL, Digital Electronic Circuits (Prof. Goutam Saha, IIT Kharagpur)
sources.note: read from the opening to the two-variable map and its minterm numbering, plus the closing summary: the truth table rewritten as a grid, the A/B axis reading, the minterm numbering m0..m3, the first grouping (AB' + AB = A), and the summary's four rules - logical adjacency is the whole method, SOP covers every 1 with the fewest and largest power-of-two groups, POS covers the 0s, and a don't care is treated as 0 or 1 according to which makes the group larger. The middle of the transcript was not served, so the 3- and 4-variable worked examples are not attributed to it.

sources.note: read the K Map, Min Sum of Products Form and Min Products of Sum Form sections: the grouping rules (powers of two, rectangular, wrap-around, every 1 covered, largest groups first), the definitions of prime implicant and essential prime implicant, the don't-care rule, and the three-step algorithm for a minimal SOP (circle the PIs, take all EPIs, then a minimum subset for the rest). Used as the GATE-oriented statement of the rules, not as a source of questions.

sourceLine: The grouping rules and the cover requirement: NPTEL IIT Kharagpur Digital Electronic Circuits Lecture 10 closing summary (English) - logical adjacency is the key, every 1 is covered by the fewest and largest power-of-two groups. The reading rule (keep the constant variables): GATE Overflow's Digital Logic subject notes (English, read in part) and recomputation in scripts/validate.py.
